bivy.name: The Notch
bivy.water: A small source roughly two hundred feet below the col; nothing running at the camp itself, and parties who stop lower on Shannon Ridge report no surface water at all and carry it up
bivy.capacity: A handful of small parties on the flats either side of the col
bivy.permit: The notch lies inside the park boundary, so an overnight here needs a North Cascades backcountry permit for the Sulphide cross-country zone, and the park's food-storage rule applies
bivy.notes: The first place worth stopping, where the ridge crest gives out against the mountainside around 5,400-5,500 ft. It is the low-commitment choice and leaves a long summit day: everything above, including the glacier and the summit pyramid, is still ahead of you.

bivy.name: Lower bivy site
bivy.water: Running water is usual here through the summer once the snow pulls back, and it is the last dependable source — parties heading higher fill up around 6,000 ft rather than counting on the upper site
bivy.capacity: Several tents; reports describe numerous bare, snow-free platforms by mid-July
bivy.permit: Inside the Sulphide cross-country zone, so a park backcountry permit is required; the composting toilet is only usable once it melts out and blue bags are the fallback
bivy.notes: The site most parties use, at roughly 6,100-6,200 ft where the ridge broadens toward the glacier toe. It has a composting toilet, it melts out earlier than the upper site, and it is far enough along the traverse that summit day is reasonable.

bivy.name: Upper bivy site
bivy.water: Often none — the usual arrangement is to fill bottles at the lower site and melt snow up here, though some parties have found a running trickle beside the upper toilet late in a warm season
bivy.capacity: Room for more than one party along the ridgeline, but expect to level a platform in snow
bivy.permit: Also inside the Sulphide cross-country zone and subject to the same park permit and food-storage requirement; a composting toilet sits on the ridgeline when melted out
bivy.notes: About a thousand feet above the col at the edge of the Sulphide Glacier, roughly 6,400 ft. It shortens summit day the most and holds snow far later, so plan on camping on snow and on a colder, windier night than the lower site.

bivy.name: Boston Basin high camp
bivy.water: Meltwater streams off the Quien Sabe Glacier and the snowfields above the basin; strongest early in the season and thinner by late summer
bivy.capacity: A designated cluster of hardened sites shared with everyone climbing Forbidden, Sharkfin and Boston — it fills on summer weekends
bivy.permit: A North Cascades backcountry permit is required, and camping in the basin is legal only at the two designated sites. Permits are picked up in person at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount and carry a per-person fee plus a reservation fee; demand outstrips supply on peak weekends
bivy.notes: The upper of the basin's two camps, around 6,400 ft, with a composting toilet. It is the natural base for the Quien Sabe: the glacier starts more or less at the tent door, so summit day is short. Snow lingers here well into July, and the rule to pitch only on hardened ground matters — the meadows recover very slowly.

bivy.name: Boston Basin low camp
bivy.water: Creeks draining the basin run past the camp through the climbing season
bivy.capacity: The second designated site, with its own composting toilet; a fallback when the upper sites are taken
bivy.permit: Same park backcountry permit and the same designated-sites-only rule as the high camp
bivy.notes: Around 5,300 ft on the edge of a moraine crest among small trees, below the polished slabs the Quien Sabe has left behind. Melts out earlier and is more sheltered than the high camp, at the cost of an extra thousand feet on summit morning.

bivy.name: Boston Basin high camp
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams below the Quien Sabe Glacier; reliable early, patchier late in a dry summer
bivy.capacity: One of only two legal camping areas in the basin, shared with parties bound for Forbidden, Sharkfin, Sahale and Buckner
bivy.permit: Overnights need a North Cascades backcountry permit, collected at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center, and camping is restricted to the two designated sites; the basin is popular enough that summer weekends often have nothing left
bivy.notes: The upper camp, roughly 6,400 ft, with a composting toilet. It is the practical base for Boston: from here you gain the Quien Sabe and traverse under Sharkfin toward the peak's east side. The rock on this route is notoriously rotten, so most parties climb it unroped to keep out from under each other, and having camp close by is what keeps the exposure time short.

bivy.name: Boston Basin low camp
bivy.water: Basin creeks run beside the site
bivy.capacity: The basin's second designated area, also with a composting toilet
bivy.permit: Same park permit and designated-sites-only restriction as the high camp
bivy.notes: About 5,300 ft on a morainal rib with a little tree cover. Slower parties and early-season trips use it because it melts out sooner and is more sheltered; the trade is a longer summit day.

bivy.name: Sahale Glacier Camp
bivy.water: Streams of glacier runoff beside the camp; filter it. Late in a dry season the flow can be some distance down the moraine
bivy.capacity: A small number of built tent pads, each inside a low dry-stone wall — the walls exist because nothing shelters this ridge from wind. It is one of the most sought-after sites in the park
bivy.permit: A North Cascades backcountry permit is required and is picked up in person at the Marblemount ranger station; the site is in heavy demand and reservations go through the park's lottery and booking system
bivy.notes: Around 7,600 ft at the end of the Sahale Arm trail, about six miles and 4,000 ft from Cascade Pass trailhead. It is the standard base for the southwest side of Buckner: from camp you drop east onto Sahale's southeast ridge, scramble down easy ground to a snow finger, and cross into Horseshoe Basin before starting up. Marine fog rolling through the camp overnight is common and can leave you with no view of the objective until morning.

bivy.name: Upper Horseshoe Basin bivy
bivy.water: Snowmelt in the basin; a matter of what is running when you arrive rather than a fixed source
bivy.capacity: Informal — a party or two levelling a spot on slabs or snow, with no facilities of any kind
bivy.notes: A cross-country alternative used by parties who would rather not depend on a Sahale Glacier Camp permit: descend into the upper basin and sleep on whatever ground you reach. The basin is a mix of clean granite slabs, snow patches and loose rock, and the lower basin is the awkward part to travel. It puts you at the foot of the southwest slopes, but it is genuinely primitive and the slabs that look flat rarely are.

bivy.name: Meadows north of Park Creek Pass
bivy.water: Creeks and snowmelt in the meadows below the pass
bivy.capacity: Open flat ground rather than built sites; a few parties at a time
bivy.permit: Everything on this route is inside North Cascades National Park, so an overnight needs a park backcountry permit and the itinerary is built night by night from designated camps and cross-country zones
bivy.notes: Broad sandy meadows a short way north of Park Creek Pass, which itself sits near 6,100 ft. This is where the long valley walk finally ends and the climbing terrain starts; parties either stop here or push the last 500 ft into the moraine above.

bivy.name: Moraine camp above the pass
bivy.water: Snowmelt off the glacier remnant beside the moraine
bivy.capacity: A sheltered flat big enough for a few tents
bivy.permit: Inside the park; covered by the same backcountry permit as the rest of the route
bivy.notes: Roughly 6,350 ft, gained by turning east from the meadows and climbing about 500 ft into the moraine of the glacier remnant. Flat, sandy and better protected than the open meadows, and the usual high camp for the Fremont Glacier. From here the route traverses about two miles north around a broad ridge over heather and rock to reach the glacier near 8,000 ft.

bivy.name: Fremont Glacier saddle
bivy.water: Running water reported nearby in season
bivy.capacity: A party or two on rock outcrops; no shelter of any kind
bivy.permit: Inside the park and inside a cross-country zone, so it must be on the permit like every other night
bivy.notes: The highest option, on outcrops at the glacier's edge around 8,000 ft, about two miles past Park Creek Pass. It makes for the shortest summit day but commits you to a fully exposed alpine camp, and getting there is a long day in its own right from the valley.

bivy.name: Valley camps on the walk in
bivy.water: Thunder Creek and Park Creek run beside these camps
bivy.capacity: Established backcountry sites with a fixed number of parties each
bivy.permit: Designated North Cascades camps, reserved by name for specific nights on the backcountry permit; Stehekin-side parties can obtain the permit at the ranger station there
bivy.notes: The approach is long enough that most parties sleep at least one night in the forest before reaching climbing terrain — Thunder Basin in the upper Thunder Creek drainage from the Colonial Creek side, or Buckner Camp on Park Creek (named for the mountain, not on it) coming in from Stehekin. Park Creek has to be crossed near some of these camps and is worth doing in daylight.

bivy.name: Wing Lake
bivy.water: The lake itself, right at camp, all season
bivy.capacity: A site at the lake outlet plus several more on benches above it; the basin is quiet compared with the Maple Pass loop below, and parties regularly have it to themselves midweek
bivy.permit: No backcountry permit is described for camping here — the approach and the lake are on national forest land — but a Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass is needed to park at Rainy Pass
bivy.notes: The standard base camp for Black Peak, roughly 6,900 ft in a basin of scree and boulders directly beneath the peak, with larches around the shore that turn gold in late September. It sits about 1,200 ft above Lewis Lake, reached by a rough boot path over a boulder field with one steep step. Nights are cold — near freezing even in good weather — and from here the South Ridge scramble is a half-day round trip. The better tent spots are in the larch groves just below the lake.

bivy.name: Lewis Lake
bivy.water: The lake, though it runs silty
bivy.capacity: At least one good site just above the lake beside the path, and room for a small party or two
bivy.permit: Same as Wing Lake: no overnight permit described, parking pass required at the trailhead
bivy.notes: About 5,700 ft, the first lake past Heather Pass and the lower fallback if the light goes or the boulder field above looks unappealing. It is a legitimate base — parties do summit and return from here — but it adds 1,200 ft each way to summit day, and the bugs are worse than higher up.

bivy.name: Leroy Basin
bivy.water: Leroy Creek and the meadow springs in the basin
bivy.capacity: An open flat basin rather than numbered sites — several parties fit, and it is shared with everyone climbing Seven Fingered Jack
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness: the wilderness permit is free and self-issued at the trailhead register, and a Northwest Forest Pass is needed to park
bivy.notes: A flat meadow basin near 6,100 ft, reached by leaving the Phelps Creek trail where it crosses Leroy Creek around 4,100 ft and taking the steep unmaintained climbers' path up the creek's north side. It is the usual base on this side of the range, and the north side of Maude is gained from here by continuing south-southeast toward the col below the peak and dropping to the Entiat Glacier. Camp on durable ground — the meadows are the reason the basin is worth camping in.

bivy.name: Upper Ice Lake
bivy.water: The lake, which can still be partly frozen early in the season
bivy.capacity: Open pumice flats with room for several parties, at the south end of the lake
bivy.permit: Also in the Glacier Peak Wilderness, with the same free self-issued permit; the standard guidance is to pitch on the pumice and keep off the meadows
bivy.notes: The higher of two lakes in a pumice basin directly under the peak, about a mile and 400 ft above Lower Ice Lake, near the 6,900 ft high point of the Ice Creek trail. Parties climbing the north face camp on the snow-free ground at the lake's south end and start around four in the morning, dropping from the lake onto the slopes beside the face and climbing to the glacier; reckon on about four hours from the edge of the Entiat Glacier to the summit. It can be reached from Leroy Basin by the climbers' path heading south, or from the long Entiat River approach.
